49	\section{Automatic Widening}
50	\seclabel{widening}
51	
52	\begin{Grammar}
53	\emph{Coercion} &::=&
54	\KWD{coerce}\option{\emph{StaticParams}}\texttt(\emph{BindId} \emph{IsType}\texttt)\emph{CoercionClauses} \KWD{widens} \EXP{=} \emph{Expr}\\
55	
56	\end{Grammar}
57	
58	
59	Fortress supports what is sometimes called ``widest-need'' evaluation
60	of numerical expressions.  To see the problem, suppose that \VAR{a}
61	and \VAR{b} are 32-bit floating-point numbers and \VAR{c} is a 64-bit
62	floating-point number.  It is easy, and tempting, to write an
63	expression such as
64	%% c = c + a \cdot b
65	\begin{Fortress}
66	\(c = c + a \cdot b\)
67	\end{Fortress}
68	but if you stop to think about it, if interpreted naively it will
69	compute the product \EXP{a \cdot b} as a 32-bit floating-point number,
70	and the impression that the sum may be accurate to the precision of a
71	64-bit floating-point number is only an illusion.  Widest-need
72	processing takes context into account and ``widens'' (or ``upgrades'')
73	the operands \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} to 64-bit floating-point numbers
74	before the product is computed, so that the product will be computed
75	as a 64-bit result.
76	
77	Before widening is considered, a Fortress compiler,
78	in its normal course of operation, analyzes
79	an expression bottom-up.  For every functional invocation, it needs
80	to statically identify a specific declaration to be invoked.
81	Once this is done, then for %every argument position of
82	every functional invocation, one of two conditions holds:
83	(a) The type of the argument expression is a subtype of the
84	    type of the parameter in the identified declaration.
85	(b) The type of the argument expression can be coerced to the
86	    type of the parameter in the identified declaration.
87	
88	This process has to be done bottom-up because in order to select a
89	specific declaration for a functional invocation, it is necessary to
90	know the types of the argument expressions, and if an argument
91	expression is itself a functional invocation, it is necessary to
92	select the specific declaration for that invocation in order to find
93	out the return type of the invocation.
94	
95	Once an expression has been fully analyzed in this way, then widening
96	is performed as a top-down process.  For each functional invocation
97	that appears in a context where a coercion can occur, ask
98	whether the argument expression (which, remember, is a functional invocation)
99	falls under case (a) or case (b) above.  If case (b), coercion of the
100	functional result is required; if the relevant coercion declaration is
101	a ``widening'' coercion, then this functional invocation is a
102	candidate for widening.  Call the type of the functional invocation
103	\VAR{T}, and call the expected type of the coercion context, \VAR{U}.
104	
105	
106	When the functional call was considered during the bottom-up analysis,
107	in general many overloaded declarations may have been considered; of
108	all those that were applicable with coercion
109	to the static call, the most specific one was chosen.
110	When considering widening, we consider the same set of declarations, but
111	first discard all declarations whose return types are not subtypes of
112	\VAR{U}.  Then if any remain, and there is a unique most specific one
113	among them, then that declaration is attached to the functional call
114	instead.  In this way a coercion step is eliminated (coercion is no
115	longer needed to convert the result of the functional invocation from
116	type \VAR{T} to type \VAR{U}), possibly at the expense of requiring
117	a new coercion in a subexpression---but this is exactly the desired
118	effect.  Once this is done, then the subexpressions of the functional
119	call are processed recursively.
120	
121	
122	This process is general enough not only to provide for
123	widening floating-point precision, but to handle two other cases
124	of interest as well: widening point computations to interval computations,
125	and widening computations involving aggregate data structures whose
126	components are widenable.  For example, in \EXP{d (v \times w)} suppose that
127	\VAR{d} is of type $\mathbb{R}64$ and \VAR{v} and \VAR{w} are 3-vectors with components
128	of type $\mathbb{R}32$; this strategy is capable of promoting \VAR{v} and \VAR{w}
129	to 3-vectors with components of type $\mathbb{R}64$ and then performing all
130	computations with $\mathbb{R}64$ precision.
131	
132	Let's go through the example of \EXP{c + a \cdot b} in detail.
133	The relevant declarations might look something like this:
134	%trait RR32
135	%  ...
136	%end
137	%
138	%trait RR64
139	%  coerce(x:RR32) widens = ...
140	%  ...
141	%end
142	
143	%opr DOT(l: RR32, r: RR32): RR32 = ... (* 1 *)
144	%opr DOT(l: RR64, r: RR64): RR64 = ... (* 2 *)
145	%opr +(l: RR32, r: RR32): RR32 = ... (* 3 *)
146	%opr +(l: RR64, r: RR64): RR64 = ... (* 4 *)
147	\begin{Fortress}
148	\(\KWD{trait}\:\mathbb{R}32\)\\
149	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
150	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
151	\(\KWD{trait}\:\mathbb{R}64\)\\
152	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(x\COLONOP\mathbb{R}32) \KWD{widens}\: = \ldots\)\\
153	\(  \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
154	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
155	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\cdot}(l\COLON \mathbb{R}32, r\COLON \mathbb{R}32)\COLON \mathbb{R}32 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  1 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
156	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\cdot}(l\COLON \mathbb{R}64, r\COLON \mathbb{R}64)\COLON \mathbb{R}64 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  2 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
157	\(\KWD{opr} +(l\COLON \mathbb{R}32, r\COLON \mathbb{R}32)\COLON \mathbb{R}32 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  3 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
158	\(\KWD{opr} +(l\COLON \mathbb{R}64, r\COLON \mathbb{R}64)\COLON \mathbb{R}64 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  4 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)
159	\end{Fortress}
160	
161	The bottom-up analysis observes that \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} are both of type
162	\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, and discovers that declarations \EXP{1} and \EXP{2}
163	are both applicable to the product, but declaration \EXP{1}
164	would be chosen because it requires no coercion and declaration \EXP{2}
165	would require coercion of both arguments to type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
166	The analysis then observes that \VAR{c} has type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
167	and the product expression has type \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, so declaration
168	\EXP{3} is not applicable but declaration \EXP{4} is applicable
169	(though requiring a coercion from \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} for its second argument).
170	
171	Now the top-down widening analysis is performed.  The product is
172	a functional call that is an argument to another functional call,
173	and its result requires coercion, and that coercion is a widening
174	coercion.  Therefore the compiler reconsiders the applicable
175	declarations, which were declarations \EXP{1} and \EXP{2}.
176	The result type of declaration \EXP{1} is not a subtype
177	of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, but the result type of declaration \EXP{2}
178	is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (in fact, it \emph{is} \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}).
179	Declaration \EXP{2} is the most specific among the applicable declarations
180	with that property (in fact, in this example it's the only one),
181	so declaration \EXP{2} replaces declaration \EXP{1} for the
182	product invocation.  This in turn requires \VAR{a} and \VAR{b}
183	to be coerced from type \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
184	before the product is performed.
185	
186	Widening is a tricky business, best left to expert library designers.
187	When used judiciously, it can greatly improve the precision of
188	numerical computations without requiring a great deal of thought on
189	the part of the application programmer and without cluttering up code
190	with explicit conversions.
191	
192	\emph{Future versions of this specification will include tables of
193	  coercions and widening coercions supported by \library.}

355	## 6. `RR32` a sibling of `RR64`
356	
357	The fork: whether anything in the library or the corpus argues for keeping `RR32` below `RR64`, against the specification, the later Types chapter, the team's 2009 commit and the compiler library (`explorations/reviews/batch-6-conformance.md`, finding 3).
358	
359	The prototype, `probes/rr32/rr32-sibling.patch`, library only: `value object RR32 extends { Number, StandardPartialOrder[\RR32\], StandardMinMax[\RR32\], AdditiveGroup[\RR32\], MultiplicativeRing[\RR32\] }`, the algebra `RR64` carries at its own type; every `b:RR64` parameter of `RR32`'s natives made `b:RR32` (row 435's second fix) and its `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX` answering `RR32`; `RR64` excluding `RR32`, no longer comprising it, and declaring `coerce(x: RR32) = asFloat(x)`, as the compiler library's `RR64` does (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:433-435`); `Number` comprising `RR32`. Three library sites needed more on the way, each recorded in the patch:
360	- `RR32`'s `^(self, b:ZZ64):RR32`, beside `^(self, b:Number):RR64`, broke the return-type rule once `RR32` is no longer an `RR64`, and so did `MultiplicativeRing`'s `^(self, other:AnyIntegral): T` beside the `Number` form; the prototype gives `RR32` one `^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR32` on its own native and drops the other two integer forms.
361	- `Number`'s `=` compares a float with any number after `asFloat`, but tests for a float by `typecase ... RR64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:358-365`); the prototype adds the `RR32` case, since an `RR32` would otherwise fall to `exactValue` and compare as 0/0.
362	
363	`RR32Micro.fss`: on the base (`RR32Micro.base.txt`) an `RR32` value is an `RR64` in a `typecase`, and `a + 2.5` ends the run with `InterpreterBug: getRR32 not implemented for FFloatLiteral` (row 435). On the prototype (`RR32Micro.sibling.txt`) the value is an `RR32` and not an `RR64`; `a + b` is an `RR32` 4.0; `a + 2.5` and `2.5 + a` are 4.0 and `a + 2` is 3.5, by `RR64`'s arithmetic after the coercion, which is the specification's worked example (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:861-898`); and an `RR32` passed to an `RR64` parameter converts.
364	
365	**What the first shape missed.** `RR32`'s api declares its getters, one `^` and `MINNUM`/`MAXNUM` only (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:47-74`); its other operators are declared in the component alone. An operator `RR32` shares with `RR64` through an algebra trait (`+`, `-`, `DOT`, `TIMES`, juxtaposition, `^`, `MIN`, `MAX`) reaches `RR32`'s own declaration through the trait's. The rest (`/`, `SQRT`, the `_UP`, `_DOWN` and `IEEE_` forms, `|self|`, `floor`, `ceiling`, `truncate` and the others) are visible to a program only as `RR64`'s functional methods, which `RR64`'s api declares (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:313-372`). On the base an `RR32` is an `RR64`, so `RR64`'s `/` dispatches on its receiver to `RR32`'s; with the first shape `a / b` converts both `RR32` operands to `RR64` and answers an `RR64` (`probes/rr32/RR32Div2.fss`, `RR32Div2.sibling.txt`: `/`, `SLASH_UP`, `PLUS_UP` and `SQRT` answer `RR64`, the other five `RR32`).
366	
367	**The second shape**, `probes/rr32/rr32-sibling-api.patch`, is the first plus 46 lines in `RR32`'s api declaring the operators its component defines, in `RR64`'s form (it applies to 2851e5086). With it all nine operators of `RR32Div2` answer `RR32` (`RR32Div2.sibling-api.txt`), and `RR32Micro` answers as with the first shape except that `SQRT a` is now `RR32`'s own, `1.2247449`, where the first shape computed it as an `RR64` (`RR32Micro.sibling-api.txt`).
368	
369	**The corpus passes.** Rung F's three passes (`count-run.sh`, one JVM per test and private caches; `compare-normalised.py`, batch 5's normalisation) over the 414 files of `ProjectFortress/tests/` at 2851e5086, their machine lines and times in `probes/rr32/passes-machine.txt`: base A (30 minutes), base B and the first shape's edit (34 minutes each, run side by side), then the second shape's edit after them.
370	- The first shape (`probes/rr32/compare-sibling.txt`): 386 the same, 7 equal once normalised (library lines the edit moved), 17 unstable (the two base passes differ: timings, random data, task traces), and 4 changed. `XXXRR32MixedRungF` passes (exit 1 to 0), row 435's expected failure, which the rung promotes. `testRR32`, a team test, fails at its line 30, `infinity: RR32 = narrow(1.0) / narrow(0.0)`, "RHS expression type Float is not assignable to LHS type RR32": the missing api declarations above. `XXXArrayLiteralArgRungC` keeps its verdict, and its message lists `RR32`'s own `-` among the candidates where it listed `RR64`'s. `XXXInheritedOverload` names its two declarations in the other order, which its row calls unstable (row 430).
371	- The second shape (`probes/rr32/compare-sibling-api.txt`; 10 minutes, the load 2.2 at its start against 10 to 13 for the others): 387 the same, 7 equal once normalised, the same 17 unstable, and 3 changed, each keeping the verdict the rung expects. `XXXRR32MixedRungF` passes (row 435's expected failure). `XXXArrayLiteralArgRungC` keeps its verdict, and its message lists `RR32`'s own `-` and `RR32`'s instance of `AdditiveGroup`'s `-` among the candidates, where it listed `RR64`'s `-` with `RR32` in its receiver's type. `XXXCoercionTupleOverloadRungC` keeps its verdict and prints its two `pair` declarations in the other order, a set's order and not a property of the program, as in row 430's message. `testRR32` passes, as on the base, and no other output changes.

6	
7	The one library already solves this problem the same way five times, never on an integer type:
8	
9	- `TotalComparison` declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`, with exactly `StandardTotalOrder`'s bodies at its own type (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:172-175`, api `.fsi:129-131`), under the team's comment "Avoid ambiguity between the default definitions of CMP and >=" (`:161-163`). The three are the revival's, added by climb batch 7 rung H; the comment is the team's (provenance below).
10	- `RR64` (`.fss:427-429`, api `.fsi:326-328`) and `QQ` (`.fss:582-591`, api `.fsi:412-414`) declare all three at their own type, beside the ones they inherit from `StandardMinMax`.
11	- `Float` and `RR32` in `FortressBuiltin` declare them in the component only, on natives (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:93-99`, `:261-268`).
12	- Other operators of the same family use the same device. `ZZ64` declares `>`, `>=`, `<=` and `CMP` itself (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:788-794`) under the team's comment "Argh! Due to method ambiguities with ZZ, these definitions must be given explicitly here." (`:786-787`). `ZZ` declares `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP` (`:943-947`).
13	
14	Outside the one library, the same device appears three more times:
15	- The compiler library declares all three on every integer type and on `IntLiteral` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:137-139`, `:198-200`, `:261-263`, `:318-320`, `:378-380`, `:425-427`; bodies at `CompilerBuiltin.fss:552-554`, `:649-651`, `:738-740`, `:803-805`, `:869-871`). It does so on `ZZ32` although `ZZ32` also extends `StandardTotalOrder[\ZZ32\]` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:210`).
16	- The team's unfinished draft declares `MAX` and `MIN` on `ZZ` and `QQ`, and `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM` beside them on `ZZ` (`Library/incomplete/basic/Fortress.Number.fsi:144-147`, `:43-44`).
17	- The specification's `ZZ` declares `MAX`, `MIN`, `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM`, and no `MINMAX` (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:263-266`).
18	
19	Provenance, by `git blame` at the base (`bce66f1fa`):
20	- The team's, present at the history's earliest reachable commit (`5a68404fd`, 2012-07-19): `StandardTotalOrder`'s bodies (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:285-288`), `QQ`'s own three (`:582-587`), the comment over `TotalComparison` (`:161-163`), the compiler library's declarations and bodies, the draft's and the specification's.
21	- The team's device, retyped by the revival: `RR64`'s (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:427-429`), `Float`'s and `RR32`'s (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:95-99`, `:263-268`) are declared at `Number` in `5a68404fd` and were retyped to `RR64` by climb batch 6 rung F in `d846e3644` (2026-09-27).

23	
24	So the precedent followed is the team's: `StandardTotalOrder`'s bodies (`:285-288`) at the type's own type, as `QQ` declares its own three (`:582-587`) and as the compiler library declares all three on every integer type. `TotalComparison`'s three are the revival's restatement of the same device.
